questions.prompt: What is Chapter 11's main claim about distribution?
choices: Distribution is a core competence of a business
Distribution matters only after a company stops improving the product
Distribution is mostly hype wrapped around weak products

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats distribution as part of how value reaches customers.
explanation.direct: Its core claim is that distribution belongs inside the serious work of building a business.
explanation.competitive: Reach is not side work. It is core work.

questions.prompt: Why is product quality alone not enough in this chapter?
choices: Because quality is less important than branding
Because customers still need a path to the product
Because great products usually get worse when they sell

explanation.gentle: The chapter says a good product still has to reach people somehow.
explanation.direct: Quality does not erase the separate problem of customer access.
explanation.competitive: A strong build still dies if nobody can get to it.

questions.prompt: What limit keeps the chapter from collapsing into hype?
choices: Distribution matters because access matters, not because promotion replaces quality
The best sales strategy is to ignore the product
Only products with weak quality need distribution

explanation.gentle: The chapter defends reach without treating hype as a substitute for real value.
explanation.direct: Its boundary is that distribution supports a strong product instead of replacing one.
explanation.competitive: The answer is a real route, not louder noise.

questions.prompt: Priya's team built the better product, but the weaker competitor keeps winning users. Which lesson fits best?
choices: The better product should wait longer for organic discovery
A weaker product can still win if its route to customers is stronger
Product quality and market reach are the same problem

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the better build can still lose when distribution is worse.
explanation.direct: Priya is seeing the difference between product strength and go-to-market strength.
explanation.competitive: The market is rewarding the route, not just the build.

questions.prompt: Why should Owen's demo-day team spend time on reach instead of only polishing the project?
choices: Because polish never matters once the product works
Because the right people still need to encounter the project
Because demo-day judges prefer weaker but louder projects

explanation.gentle: The team still has to make sure real people can see and evaluate the work.
explanation.direct: Reach is part of success because quality hidden from the audience has limited effect.
explanation.competitive: An invisible upgrade is still invisible.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat sales as strategic rather than secondary?
choices: Because sales makes product quality irrelevant
Because sales and channels help carry value into the market
Because technical teams should avoid customer contact

explanation.gentle: The chapter says sales matters because it helps connect the product to customers.
explanation.direct: Sales is strategic here because it is part of the route from value to use.
explanation.competitive: No selling path means trapped value.

questions.prompt: Why do channels matter in Chapter 11?
choices: They shape how customers first encounter and adopt the product
They mainly add status to the company after growth starts
They reduce the need for a useful product

explanation.gentle: Channels help determine how the product reaches people in the first place.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats channel design as part of the mechanism that turns value into market reality.
explanation.competitive: The route shapes whether attention becomes use.

questions.prompt: Lena built a thoughtful project, but almost nobody finds it. What does the chapter suggest she is missing?
choices: A real path from the project to the people who might care
A lower-quality version that spreads more easily
Proof that quality never matters

explanation.gentle: The project may be good, but people still need a route to it.
explanation.direct: Lena's problem is access, not necessarily product value.
explanation.competitive: The work is real. The route is weak.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter connect product strength and go-to-market strength?
choices: They are identical if the product is strong enough
A company must solve both because they are different strengths
Go-to-market strength matters only when product strength is weak

explanation.gentle: The chapter says both strengths matter because building and reaching are not the same task.
explanation.direct: A company can be right about the product and still weak at getting it to customers.
explanation.competitive: Winning the build does not guarantee winning the route.

choices: It shifts from distribution toward how people and technology work together inside delivery systems
It concludes that humans should step aside completely once channels are built
It returns from business design to culture perks

explanation.gentle: Once the route to customers matters, the next question is how people and technology share the work inside that route.
explanation.direct: The bridge moves from distribution to human-machine complementarity.
explanation.competitive: The next chapter asks who should actually carry each part of the system.
